unit: per job: the serviceable fuel filter (on a diesel pickup, both the frame-mounted and the engine-mounted filter), fitted. Many newer gasoline cars have no separately serviceable fuel filter: the filter is inside the in-tank fuel pump module and is not serviced on its own, so this job does not apply to them (see fuel pump replacement). Not included: diagnosis, fuel line or housing repairs, water-in-fuel sensors

finding: New job, so there is no live range to compare, and this file is HELD: it is not complete enough to show. First, who it applies to: many modern gasoline cars have no serviceable fuel filter at all (the filter is a strainer inside the in-tank fuel pump module; one benchmark notes that many modern gas cars use 'lifetime' in-tank strainers and that some makers are dropping external filters), so the job is built only on vehicles that do have one: older gasoline cars with a separate filter, some European cars, and diesels, where the filters are routine maintenance. What could be built (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): truck 2017 Ford F-250 6.7L diesel, both filters, about $201-$304 (Motorcraft kit $81.45 at a retailer to $143.62 genuine list, 1.0 hr). Partly built, top end only: economy 2007 Ford Focus up to about $195 (genuine filter list $35.45 plus 1.0 hr at $160; with the 0.5 hr low end, labor alone is $60); luxury 2005 Mercedes-Benz C240 up to about $294 (genuine filter list $54.00 plus 1.5 hr at $160; labor alone at the 0.75 hr low end is $90). These sit in the same region as the benchmarks (FIXD $86-$182, Jerry $80-$300 for gas cars and $150-$450 for diesels, RepairPal $258-$322). How solid the labor times are: none is a manufacturer time. Searches of maker bulletins (GM Duramax, Ram Cummins, Nissan Titan XD Cummins) found fuel-filter procedures but no printed time for a filter change. The truck time is a parts seller's approximate 1 hour for both filters on the example truck; the luxury time is a repair-manual publisher's do-it-yourself 0h45-1h30 for the example car's generation (the same publisher prints 0h45 for a BMW Z3 and 3h30 for a BMW Z4, so European cars vary a lot); the economy time is a general 30-60 minute do-it-yourself figure that is not vehicle-specific. Why it is held: (1) the midsize class has no example vehicle, parts price or stated time; (2) the economy and luxury classes have no usable low parts price: the cheaper prices seen (a discounted genuine Focus filter at $22.72; Bosch and Hengst filters for the C240 at $50.99) are on pages that do not state the part's condition, so they are recorded as cross-checks only, leaving each class with one usable parts figure; (3) no class has a manufacturer-stated labor time. A second pass on 2026-11-20 did not clear these. Cheaper filters were found for the Focus (WIX $12.06 and K&N $15.40 at a parts retailer, Motorcraft $29.95 at a Ford specialist) and for the C240 (Hengst $38.92 on a page for the 2004 car, Hengst $54.99 elsewhere), but none of those pages states that the part is new; the one page that does (an unbranded filter at $21.43 on a marketplace) is not a known-quality brand, so the lows stay null. More maker bulletins were loaded (Chrysler/Ram Cummins, Nissan Titan XD, Isuzu, Hino, Detroit, PACCAR): the only times printed were for add-on filtration kits (Ram: 1.0 Hr suggested for a severe-duty kit) or for larger repairs that include the filters, never for a routine filter change. One aftermarket seller that states condition could not be read for these filters because its pages refused automated loading. To finish: pick a midsize example with a separate filter, load an aftermarket filter price for each class from a page that states the part is new, and look for a maker-printed time (diesel maintenance bulletins are the most likely place). This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds: diagnosis if the filter is being changed to chase a symptom (hard starting, hesitation, a fuel-pressure code); new sealing washers, O-rings or line clips; shop supplies and a fuel disposal fee; sales tax. On diesels: a water-in-fuel sensor or drain valve, priming or bleeding the fuel system, and resetting the filter-life monitor; diesel filters are due far more often than gasoline ones (the example truck's interval is 22,500 miles, or 15,000 miles in severe service). On rusty older vehicles, seized fuel line fittings can turn a short job into a line repair. On cars whose filter is part of the in-tank pump module, the fix is a fuel pump module replacement, a much larger job.
